question: Which statement best describes figure and figcaption?
options: <video> embeds playable video. Give it controls so users get play/pause/volume, width/height (or CSS) to reserve layout space, and a src or nested <source> elements. Set muted if you need autoplay to be allowed, and provide a poster image for the pre-play state. Always include captions via <track> for accessibility.

<audio> embeds sound — podcasts, clips, music. Like video it takes controls, src or nested <source>, preload, loop, and muted. There is no poster (audio has no frame), but you should still provide a transcript or descriptive text for accessibility, since deaf/hard-of-hearing users can't hear the content.

Browsers support different codecs, so list several <source> children with type attributes; the browser picks the first it can play. Provide widely supported formats (MP4/H.264 and WebM for video; MP3 and OGG for audio). Put fallback text after the sources for browsers that can't play any. The type attribute lets the browser skip formats it can't decode without downloading them.

poster is a placeholder image shown before video playback. preload hints how much to fetch: "none" (save bandwidth), "metadata" (just duration/dimensions), or "auto" (the whole file). autoplay starts playback immediately, but browsers block autoplay with sound — it only works if the video is also muted (and often playsinline). Use autoplay sparingly; it harms UX and accessibility.

<track> adds timed text to video/audio: kind="captions" or "subtitles" point to a WebVTT (.vtt) file via src, with srclang and label. Captions are essential for deaf/hard-of-hearing users and helpful for everyone in sound-off contexts. Mark the default track with the default attribute. Media without captions or a transcript fails accessibility guidelines.

question: Which statement best describes Multiple sources and formats?

Accessible media means captions/subtitles for video, transcripts for audio, no audio that autoplays loudly, and controls users can operate by keyboard. Avoid content that flashes (seizure risk). The native controls are keyboard- and screen-reader-friendly out of the box, which is a strong reason to prefer them over fully custom players unless you re-implement accessibility carefully.
